missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to describe how different domestic appliances transfer energy from batteries or ac mains to the kinetic energy of electric motors or the energy of heating devices.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson never describes how appliances transfer energy from batteries or ac mains. It does not say where the energy goes, such as the kinetic energy store of a motor or the thermal store of a heating device. It only gives power values and calculations.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to describe, with examples, the relationship between the power ratings for domestic electrical appliances and the changes in stored energy when they are in use.
missing_spec_content.why: Power ratings are listed (keyPoints[0].content, tables[1]) but are never linked to changes in stored energy. For example, a higher-power kettle transfers more energy to the water's thermal store per second.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Everyday electrical appliances are designed to bring about energy transfers.
missing_spec_content.why: This idea is not stated. The lesson treats appliances only as things that cost money to run (intro, keyPoints[2]).

above_gcse.text: P = V²/R (put I = V/R into P = IV)
above_gcse.why: The specification lists only P = VI and P = I²R as the equations to recall and apply. P = V²/R is taught as a third equation to learn, and it also appears in the tables, revisionCardBullets and checkpoint 2 feedback. This goes beyond the required equations.

above_gcse.text: Payback time = extra cost of the efficient appliance ÷ yearly saving.
above_gcse.why: Payback time is not in the specification sections given. It is tested in checkpoint 3.

above_gcse.text: For bills, electricity companies use a much larger unit: the kilowatt-hour (kWh).
above_gcse.why: The kilowatt-hour and the cost-of-electricity calculations are not in these specification sections. The specification gives energy only in joules: "energy transferred, E, in joules, J". About a third of the lesson is about content outside the specification.
Fuse ratings are not part of these specification sections. They are given without any explanation.

factual_errors.correction: This is listed under "Ways to save energy", but using appliances off-peak does not reduce the energy transferred. It may reduce cost on some tariffs only.
An 8–10 kW shower on 230 V draws about 35–45 A. It is protected by a breaker of roughly 40–45 A on a dedicated circuit, not by a 13 A fuse.

V = IR relates potential difference, current and resistance for any component. Ohm's law is the statement that current is directly proportional to potential difference for an ohmic conductor at constant temperature. Calling V = IR "Ohm's Law" is imprecise. The same label appears in tables[0].rows[0] and keyPoints[3].writeBullets[0].
